neutral_facts.value: The accused was charged with trespassing into the house of a woman and assaulting her with intent to outrage her modesty. The evidence, however, indicated that the accused had assaulted the woman's daughter-in-law to outrage her modesty. The accused defended himself against the charge of assaulting the woman and focused his cross-examination on proving that he did not assault or outrage the modesty of the woman. The prosecution's case was that the accused had touched and caught the hand of the daughter-in-law and fled when she raised an alarm. The trial court convicted the accused under sections 452 and 354 of the IPC, but the High Court upheld the conviction. The Supreme Court, however, held that the charge was incorrect as it did not mention the daughter-in-law, and the accused was not aware of the charge against her. The Court concluded that the accused was prejudiced by the error in the charge and directed a new trial after framing a charge against the daughter-in-law.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the accused could be punished for assaulting and outraging the modesty of PW1's daughter-in-law, even though he was not charged with any offence with reference to PW1's daughter-in-law, on the ground that the error or omission in the charge did not prejudice the accused or result in failure of justice.

quotes.text: The prosecution argued that the accused could be punished for assaulting and outraging the modesty of PW1's daughter-in-law, even though he was not charged with any offence with reference to PW1's daughter-in-law, on the ground that the error or omission in the charge did not prejudice the accused or result in failure of justice.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the accused was not required to defend himself against a charge that he assaulted and outraged the modesty of PW1's daughter-in-law, as the charge levelled against him was not proved, and thus he ought to have been acquitted.

quotes.text: He contended that as the charge levelled against him was not proved, and as he was not required to defend himself against a charge that he assaulted and outraged the modesty of PW1's daughter-in-law, he ought to have been acquitted.

legal_principle_applied.value: The court applied the principles of fair play and natural justice embodied in Sections 211, 212, 215 and 464 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, emphasizing that an accused should know what is the charge against him to build his defence and that the main concern is whether the accused had a fair trial.
